title: Jumbo Loans in Southern California: What's Different
description: Buying above the conforming loan limit means a jumbo loan. Learn how jumbo underwriting differs, what reserves lenders want, and how to prepare.
image_alt: A large white house with a green lawn and mature trees

faq.a: A jumbo loan is a mortgage larger than the conforming loan limit set each year by the Federal Housing Finance Agency for your county. Because Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac can't buy it, lenders set their own guidelines.

faq.q: Do jumbo loans require more cash reserves?
faq.a: Usually, yes. Jumbo lenders commonly want to see several months of housing payments in savings or retirement accounts after closing.

faq.q: Can self-employed borrowers get jumbo loans?
faq.a: Yes. Traditional jumbo loans use tax returns, and some non-QM jumbo programs allow bank statements or other alternative documentation.

body_html:
In much of Orange County and coastal Los Angeles, a "regular" family home can easily cross into jumbo territory. That surprises a lot of first-time move-up buyers who expect the process to feel the same as their last loan. It's not harder, exactly. It's just different, and knowing the differences early saves time.

What makes a loan "jumbo"

Each year, the Federal Housing Finance Agency sets conforming loan limits by county. Loans at or below the limit can be sold to Fannie Mae or Freddie Mac. Loans above it are jumbo, and each lender or investor sets its own rules. High-cost counties, including much of Southern California, have higher conforming limits than most of the country, and FHFA publishes the current figures on its conforming loan limit page.

There's also a middle ground sometimes called "high-balance" conforming, which covers loans above the national baseline but within a high-cost county's limit. If you're near the line, ask your loan officer whether you land in high-balance or jumbo, because the guidelines and pricing differ.

How jumbo underwriting differs

AreaConformingTypical jumbo
GuidelinesStandardized by Fannie Mae and Freddie MacSet by each lender or investor
ReservesOften modestCommonly several months of payments
Credit expectationsBroad range acceptedUsually stronger scores expected
AppraisalOne appraisal in most casesSometimes two on larger loans
DocumentationStandardOften more detailed, especially for complex income

Reserves: the piece people underestimate

Reserves are liquid or near-liquid assets you'll still have after closing. Jumbo lenders like to see them because larger loans carry more risk. Checking and savings count fully. Retirement accounts and brokerage accounts usually count at a percentage of their value. If your plan is to put every dollar into the down payment, talk to your loan officer first; sometimes a slightly smaller down payment with stronger reserves gets a better result.

Complex income is normal here, so plan for it

Many jumbo borrowers have RSUs, bonuses, K-1 income, or rental properties. All of that can work, but each needs documentation and history. Gather two years of tax returns, your most recent statements for every account, and vesting schedules for equity compensation before you apply. If you're self-employed and your tax returns understate your cash flow, a non-QM jumbo option using bank statements may fit better.

Strategies worth knowing about

  • Piggyback financing. A first mortgage at the conforming limit plus a second loan can sometimes cost less than one jumbo loan.
  • Relationship pricing. Some jumbo lenders offer better terms when you hold assets with them.
  • Adjustable options. For buyers who expect to move or refinance within several years, adjustable-rate jumbos can be worth comparing.

None of these is right for everyone. They're tools to compare, not defaults.

The jumbo appraisal

Unique, high-value homes can be harder to appraise because there are fewer truly comparable sales. Custom builds, view properties, and homes with significant upgrades may need more explanation. On larger loans, some lenders require a second appraisal or an additional review. Give the appraiser a clear list of upgrades and features, and make sure the home is accessible and presentable. A thoughtful appraisal process protects both the buyer's investment and the timeline.

Timing your jumbo approval

Because jumbo underwriting is more detailed, it pays to start early. Ideally, your file is reviewed before you write an offer, especially if you have complex income. Here's a sensible sequence:

  1. Share your full financial picture with your loan officer, including all accounts and income sources
  2. Get a pre-approval based on the actual jumbo program you'll use, not a generic estimate
  3. Ask whether an underwriter can review the file before you go under contract
  4. Plan your contingency timeline around jumbo underwriting, not conforming timelines

Prepared jumbo buyers can compete on equal footing with anyone. The difference is in the preparation, which my post on pre-approval covers in more detail.

The takeaway

Jumbo financing is routine in Southern California, but it rewards preparation. Know where your loan amount lands relative to the county limit, plan your reserves, and organize your income documents early. With a broker, you also get the advantage of comparing multiple jumbo investors, which matters when every lender writes its own rules.
